data.title: Urticaria & angioedema — viva
data.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Urticaria & angioedema** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define urticaria and angioedema.**
- Urticaria: transient itchy wheals — central swelling with surrounding flare, each lasting <24 h and leaving no mark — due to dermal oedema
- Angioedema: deeper swelling of dermis/subcutis/mucosa, more painful than itchy, lasting up to 72 h
- Either or both may occur

**Q2. Classify urticaria (PYQ).**
- Acute (<6 weeks) vs chronic (≥6 weeks)
- Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU): no specific trigger — autoimmune (type I autoallergic with IgE against self antigens like TPO/IL-24; type IIb autoimmune with IgG against IgE/FcεRI) or unknown
- Chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU): physical — symptomatic dermographism (commonest), cold, delayed pressure, solar, heat, vibratory; non-physical — cholinergic, contact, aquagenic
- Others/related: urticarial vasculitis, autoinflammatory syndromes (CAPS, Schnitzler), urticaria pigmentosa (mastocytosis), hereditary angioedema (no wheals)

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Mast cell degranulation (immunological IgE/autoantibody, complement C5a, neuropeptides, drugs like opioids/contrast, NSAIDs via COX-1 inhibition) → histamine, prostaglandin D2, leukotrienes, PAF, cytokines → vasodilation and vascular leak
- Bradykinin-mediated angioedema (no wheals, no itch): hereditary/acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency, ACE inhibitors

**Q4. Causes of acute urticaria.**
- Idiopathic (~50%), infections (viral URTI in children — commonest), drugs (penicillins, NSAIDs, opioids, contrast), foods (nuts, shellfish, eggs, milk), insect stings, latex, blood products

**Q5. Investigations — guideline approach.**
- Acute: none routinely unless a specific allergen is suspected
- Chronic spontaneous: limited — CBC with differential, ESR/CRP, total IgE and IgG anti-TPO (predict response to omalizumab/cyclosporine), ± basophil activation test/autologous serum skin test
- Further tests only if history suggests: thyroid function, H. pylori, stool for parasites, tryptase, skin biopsy (wheals >24 h — urticarial vasculitis), complement C4 and C1-INH for angioedema without wheals
- Provocation tests for CIndU: FricTest for dermographism, ice-cube/TempTest for cold, exercise/hot-bath for cholinergic, weighted rods for delayed pressure, phototest for solar

**Q6. Write a short note on cold urticaria (PYQ).**
- Wheals on cold exposure (cold air, water, drinks — lips/throat swelling), develop on rewarming
- Primary (acquired idiopathic) or secondary (cryoglobulins, cold agglutinins, infections — EBV, HIV, hepatitis)
- Ice-cube test: 5 min on forearm, read after 10 min — wheal positive; TempTest for threshold
- Risk: anaphylaxis/drowning with whole-body immersion (swimming) — carry epinephrine
- Treatment: avoid cold, high-dose non-sedating antihistamines, omalizumab; familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (NLRP3) is different — fever, rash, arthralgia after cold; treat with IL-1 blockers

**Q7. What is cholinergic urticaria?**
- Tiny (1–3 mm) itchy wheals with large flares after rise in core body temperature — exercise, hot shower, spicy food, emotion; young adults; sweat allergy and hypohidrosis implicated
- Exercise/hot-water test; non-sedating antihistamines, propranolol, omalizumab; exercise-induced anaphylaxis is a separate entity (food-dependent — wheat ω-5 gliadin)

**Q8. Differentiate urticaria from urticarial vasculitis.**
- Urticarial vasculitis: individual lesions last >24 h, burn/pain more than itch, leave purpura/bruising/pigmentation, systemic features (arthralgia, fever, kidney, eye, lung), low complement in hypocomplementaemic form (anti-C1q, SLE association)
- Biopsy: leukocytoclastic vasculitis; treatment — dapsone, colchicine, HCQ, steroids, immunosuppressants

**Q9. Management of chronic urticaria — the stepwise guideline.**
- Avoid triggers (NSAIDs, alcohol, tight clothing, physical triggers), treat underlying cause if found
- Step 1: standard-dose second-generation H1 antihistamine daily (cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, bilastine, desloratadine, rupatadine) — not on demand
- Step 2: increase up to 4-fold dose after 2–4 weeks if not controlled
- Step 3: add omalizumab (anti-IgE) 300 mg SC every 4 weeks (may increase dose/frequency if needed)
- Step 4: cyclosporine 3.5–5 mg/kg/day (with antihistamine) if omalizumab fails
- Short oral steroid courses (≤10 days) only for severe exacerbations; montelukast, dapsone, HCQ, H2 blockers have weak evidence
- Newer: dupilumab and the BTK inhibitor remibrutinib approved for CSU in some countries (confirm in India)

**Q10. Assessment tools.**
- UAS7 (urticaria activity score over 7 days: wheals 0–3 + itch 0–3 per day, max 42), UCT (urticaria control test, ≥12 controlled), AAS (angioedema activity), CU-Q2oL (quality of life)

**Q11. What is hereditary angioedema (HAE)?**
- Autosomal dominant deficiency (type I — low C1-INH level, ~85%) or dysfunction (type II — normal/high level but non-functional) of C1 esterase inhibitor; HAE with normal C1-INH (factor XII, plasminogen mutations, oestrogen-dependent)
- Recurrent non-itchy, non-pitting swellings of skin, gut (colic, vomiting), larynx (fatal asphyxia) without wheals; triggers — trauma, dental work, stress, oestrogens, ACE inhibitors
- Screening: low C4 (also during attacks); C1-INH level and function
- Treatment: antihistamines/steroids/adrenaline do NOT work; acute — C1-INH concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 antagonist), ecallantide, fresh frozen plasma; prophylaxis — lanadelumab (anti-kallikrein), berotralstat, C1-INH, danazol, tranexamic acid

**Q12. What is ACE-inhibitor angioedema?**
- Bradykinin accumulation from reduced breakdown — face, lips, tongue swelling without wheals; may occur after years of use; commoner in Black patients; stop the drug (also avoid ARBs cautiously); icatibant in severe cases

**Q13. How do you treat acute urticaria and anaphylaxis?**
- Acute urticaria: non-sedating antihistamine (up to 4×) ± short prednisolone course
- Anaphylaxis: adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 ml of 1:1000) IM in anterolateral thigh (child 0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg), repeat after 5 min if needed; airway, oxygen, IV fluids, then antihistamine and steroid; observe ≥6–12 h; prescribe adrenaline auto-injector

**Q14. What is dermographism?**
- Wheal along a line of firm stroking within minutes (Darier's sign is the same in mastocytosis lesions); symptomatic dermographism is the commonest CIndU — FricTest; antihistamines

**Q15. Prognosis of CSU.**
- About 50% remit in 1–5 years; severe disease, angioedema, autoimmunity and positive ASST predict longer course

## Quick spotter facts
- Individual wheal <24 h and leaves no mark = urticaria; >24 h with bruising = urticarial vasculitis
- Angioedema without wheals + abdominal pain + low C4 — HAE (no response to antihistamines)
- Step up: antihistamine ×4 → omalizumab → cyclosporine

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Urticaria); EAACI/GA²LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI urticaria guideline 2022. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
